item.title: 'As humans we feel spiritually homeless': Turkish author Ece Temelkuran on belonging
item.description: For Ece Temelkuran, the human condition is "unhomed". Speaking to FRANCE 24, the Turkish author cites the rise of artificial intelligence, climate change and the authoritarian drift as reasons why one may no longer recognise the place one calls home. This feeling of "spiritual homelessness" is something she explores in her latest book, "Nation of Strangers: Rebuilding Home in the 21st Century". Most of all, she highlights the importance of human connection: "In survival mode (...) you live on the kindness of others." Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: Artificial photosynthesis uses waste CO₂ to grow protein-rich edible fungus in seven days
item.description: While many people think first of meat when they think about dietary protein, most protein ultimately depends on plants, since livestock feed on grass, hay and other plants. item.title: Without marine life, atmospheric CO₂ would shoot up by up to 65% by the end of the century
item.description: Without marine organisms transporting carbon into the deep ocean, the accumulation of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would be drastically higher in the year 2100, reaching levels between 35% and 65% higher than projected. This is one of the main conclusions of the new policy brief developed within the framework of the European OceanICU project, which was presented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A cactus that changes gears: How the prickly pear makes the most of desert rain
item.description: In the desert, water doesn't arrive steadily. It comes in short pulses: a winter storm, a few rainy days, then months of drought. A desert plant needs two skills to live there. It has to survive the long dry spells, and it has to make full use of the brief windows when water is plentiful. A new study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and the Volcani Institute shows that the prickly pear cactus has an unexpected way of doing both. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: COP31: ¿fracaso aislado o reflejo de una crisis sistémica de las cumbres climáticas?
item.description: La cumbre para el cambio climático de las Naciones Unidas, COP31, en Antalya (Turquía) terminó sin un acuerdo político. Pero no es la primera vez que ocurre. Hace 17 años, en Copenhague, tampoco llegaron a un consenso. El fracaso llega con una serie de críticas a lo que ha sido la diplomacia climática: medidas insuficientes para lograr un cambio. Este año, algunos consideran que, incluso, fue positivo que países se hayan negado a firmar un texto que no mencione la causa fundamental de la crisis climática: los combustibles fósiles. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: Patricio Peralta

item.title: 2026, uno de los años más críticos y extremos a nivel climático
item.description: 2026 se perfila como uno de los años más alarmantes de la historia climática mundial. Durante el transcurso del año, diferentes partes del mundo han sido víctimas de fenómenos extremos como ciclones, deslizamientos, riadas, inundaciones e incendios forestales sin precedentes. Los países más vulnerables continúan siendo las naciones en desarrollo, a pesar de ser los que menos emisiones de carbono producen. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Which pollen is found in honey? Automated analysis closely matches conventional testing
item.description: Pure rapeseed honey—or not quite? Single-flower honeys must contain a certain proportion of pollen from the respective plant. This is assessed by pollen analysis, which is time-consuming and requires specialist expertise. As part of a collaborative project, a research team from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) and the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) in Leipzig worked with several partners to develop an automated, AI-based pollen analysis method for honey testing. Fuente: Phys.org.
